content: 1. Coinfections in children living with HIV can obscure the response to therapy, making diagnosis and treatment more challenging. Radiographic findings in tuberculosis (TB) often overlap with other HIV-related lung diseases, complicating the diagnostic process. 2. Integrated treatment decision algorithms for pulmonary TB (PTB) diagnosis, as outlined in Chapter 4, can be applied to children under 10 years of age living with HIV. These children are considered at higher risk for TB when presenting with PTB symptoms, and the high-risk group protocols should be followed. 3. For all children with presumptive PTB, efforts should be made to confirm the diagnosis using molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) on appropriate specimens, such as stool, nasopharyngeal aspirate, induced sputum, or gastric aspirate, depending on available equipment and expertise. 4. This diagnostic approach is particularly critical for children living with HIV who have been in contact with individuals confirmed to have drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). 5. Urine lateral flow lipoarabinomannan assay (LF-LAM) is an additional diagnostic test for children and adolescents living with HIV. This immunocapture assay detects the mycobacterial lipoarabinomannan antigen in urine and serves as a potential point-of-care test for TB in specific populations. 6. Although LF-LAM has limited sensitivity, it can be used as a rapid bedside rule-in test for TB in people living with HIV, including children and adolescents, especially in urgent cases where a quick diagnosis is critical for survival. 7. The Alere Determine TB LAM Ag is the only commercially available urine LF-LAM test endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO). 8. Children and adolescents living with HIV who exhibit signs and symptoms of PTB should have at least one specimen (e.g., stool, nasopharyngeal aspirate, sputum, or gastric aspirate in children; sputum in adolescents) submitted for mWRD testing whenever possible. 9. LF-LAM results, which are available in less than 15 minutes, can guide treatment decisions while awaiting results from other diagnostic tests. However, LF-LAM should not replace or serve as a triage test. A positive LF-LAM result is considered bacteriological confirmation of TB. 10. For children living with HIV who show signs and symptoms of extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), the guidance in Chapter 4 also applies. 11. Children living in high HIV prevalence settings or those living with HIV should be treated for TB with a four-drug regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (isoniazid and rifampicin) for four months. For non-severe TB, a shorter two-month continuation phase may be used, with standard daily dosages. 12. Eligibility for the four-month treatment regimen depends on disease severity, which can be determined using chest X-ray features or clinical criteria described in Chapter 5. 13. Children should be assessed two weeks after starting TB treatment and then reviewed monthly with clinical monitoring, including symptom assessment, weight measurement, adherence evaluation, and monitoring for adverse events. TB medication dosages should be adjusted to account for weight gain. 14. Most children living with HIV and drug-susceptible TB who adhere to treatment respond well to the six-month regimen. 15. Children living with HIV who successfully complete TB treatment may be eligible for TB preventive therapy (TPT). 16. Treatment outcomes for children living with HIV are generally poorer than for HIV-negative children. Before the widespread availability of antiretroviral therapy (ART), many deaths in children with TB/HIV coinfection occurred within the first two months of starting TB treatment. 17. Medical risk factors for poor treatment response and mortality include severe malnutrition, coinfections, severe immunosuppression, and high viral load. 18. Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for infants, children, and adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical or immune conditions. Priority should be given to children under five years old, those with severe or advanced HIV disease, and/or those with a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³. 19. In settings with high malaria or severe bacterial infection prevalence, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should continue into adulthood, regardless of ART provision. In low-prevalence settings, it may be discontinued for clinically stable children over five years old who are virally suppressed on ART for at least six months and have a CD4 count >350 cells/mm³. 20. Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is also recommended for HIV-exposed infants from 4–6 weeks of age until HIV infection is excluded through appropriate testing after breastfeeding cessation. 21. Routine cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should be provided to all people living with HIV and TB disease, regardless of CD4 count. 22. ART aims to improve the length and quality of life for children and adolescents living with HIV by reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality, decreasing opportunistic infections (including TB), lowering viral load, restoring immune function, and supporting normal growth and development. 23. ART improves TB treatment outcomes for children and adolescents living with HIV. WHO recommends initiating ART in all children and adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. 24. Rapid ART initiation (within seven days of HIV diagnosis) should be offered to all people living with HIV following a confirmed diagnosis and clinical assessment. Same-day initiation is recommended for those ready to start. 25. ART should be started as soon as possible within two weeks of initiating TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count, except in cases of meningitis, where ART should be delayed by at least four weeks and started within eight weeks. 26. Dolutegravir (DTG) is approved for use in children over four weeks old and weighing more than 3 kg. A dispersible 10 mg formulation is available. For children without approved DTG dosing, raltegravir (RAL) is an effective alternative and approved from birth, with dose adjustments during TB treatment. 27. DTG, combined with a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone, is the preferred first-line ART regimen for adolescents and children with approved DTG dosing. Low-dose efavirenz (EFV 400 mg) is an alternative first-line regimen for adolescents, except in settings with high pre-treatment HIV drug resistance to EFV or nevirapine (NVP). 28. In TB/HIV coinfection, the dose of DTG must be doubled due to drug-drug interactions with rifampicin.
